entries.title: Ukraine, South Korea relations sour over North Korean POWs
entries.summary: South Korea has accused Ukraine of breaching a confidentiality agreement over the transfer of North Korean prisoners of war — and of denying the deal's existence. Seoul has demanded an apology.
entries.content:
Ukraine

Ukraine, South Korea relations sour over North Korean POWs

September 28, 2026

South Korea has accused Ukraine of breaching a confidentiality agreement over the transfer of North Korean prisoners of war — and of denying the deal's existence. Seoul has demanded an apology.

South Korea has demanded an official apology from Ukraine after accusing Kyiv of breaching — and then reportedly denying the existence of — a confidentiality agreement regarding the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war (POWs) to Seoul.

Last week, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced the transfer in an address to the United Nations General Assembly in New York, adding that the soldiers were "not easy to capture alive."

Hours later, South Korean President Lee Jae Myung wrote on social media: "I do not know why the Ukrainian side broke the agreement and made the matter public, but it is very disappointing."

On Sunday, the South Korean consternation was made official when Seong Ghi-hong, senior presidential secretary for public relations, demanded "an official explanation and apology."

"The presidential office expresses strong regret over Ukraine's unilateral disclosure and its subsequent false announcement that there had not been a non-disclosure agreement," Seong said in a statement.

"It is in itself a very serious matter that … seriously undermines trust between the two governments and gravely damages friendly relations between the two countries."

Seong said Seoul was "considering additional measures that may be necessary regarding this matter," but did not specify what they might be.

Ukraine: When were the North Korean soldiers captured?

The North Korean soldiers were captured by Ukrainian forces in Russia's Kursk region in January 2025 — two of around 14,000 North Korean troops deployed to the area to help halt and push back a surprise Ukrainian incursion.

Ukrainian intelligence estimates that around 3,000 North Korean troops were killed and another 1,500 injured, with the rest still stationed on Russian territory. To date, no North Korean troops are believed to have operated on Ukrainian territory itself.

Ukrainian troops reported that North Korean soldiers who were surrounded or injured on the battlefield preferred to die by suicide than surrender — and only two were captured.

Under President Lee, who has attempted to improve relations with the North, South Korea has appeared hesitant to take custody of the pair. But, under Article 3 of the South Korean constitution, North Koreans are still considered citizens of the South and are permitted to live in the South.

South Korea is an ally of Ukraine, albeit one which has so far only provided non-lethal aid. But Kyiv has been pressing Seoul to provide advanced air defense systems.

Last month, President Zelenskyy claimed that up to 50,000 more North Korean troops could be deployed to Russia.

Edited by: Srinivas Mazumdaru

entries.title: Israel strips Dutch diplomats of status in West Bank
entries.summary: The move by the Israeli Foreign Ministry is a response to Dutch sanctions targeting goods from illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank. The Dutch Foreign Ministry is yet to comment.
entries.content:
Palestinian Territories

Israel strips Dutch diplomats of status in West Bank

September 28, 2026

The move by the Israeli Foreign Ministry is a response to Dutch sanctions targeting goods from illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank. The Dutch Foreign Ministry is yet to comment.

The Israeli government said on Sunday that it was revoking the diplomatic status of Dutch diplomats representing The Netherlands at the Palestinian Authority in Ramallah, the administrative capital of the Palestinian Territories.

Israeli ​Foreign Minister Gideon Saar said the move was a response to Dutch sanctions targeting illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.

"Israel will not ignore measures intended to harm it," Saar wrote on social media.

He ordered Dutch diplomats operating in Ramallah to ​return their Israeli-issued diplomatic documentation within seven days.

"After this period, the diplomatic privileges and immunities granted to them by the State of Israel will expire," he added.

Dutch ban on settlement goods: what does it entail?

Dutch authorities announced earlier this month that they would begin enforcing a ban on settlement goods.

The ban, which applies to personal baggage as well as commercial shipments, came into force on September 22 and, in recent days, Dutch and Israeli media have reported that passengers arriving at Amsterdam's Schiphol airport from Israel had their luggage searched for banned goods.

Earlier in September, Israel also ordered the closure of ⁠the British Consulate ⁠in East Jerusalem, the United Kingdom's representative to the Palestinian Authority, after London announced similar sanctions banning the import of goods from illegal settlements.

"Any country that acts in a hostile and unilateral manner against Israel will lose influence and relevance in the region," said Saar.

France and Canada have also announced a ban on goods from settlements, but Israel has not yet taken any action against ​those two countries.

In August, Israel also banned Dutch diplomats from a Israeli-based, US-led coordination center for Gaza over what the foreign minister described as "anti-Israel measures."

Edited by: Srinivas Mazumdaru

entries.title: Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic announces resignation
entries.summary: Aleksandar Vucic will now be running to be prime minister in the upcoming snap parliamentary elections slated for next month.
entries.content:
Serbia

Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic announces resignation

September 27, 2026

Aleksandar Vucic will now be running to be prime minister in the upcoming snap parliamentary elections slated for next month.

Serbia's long-time President Aleksandar Vucic announced on Sunday that he would resign from his post in order to run for prime minister in the upcoming October snap elections.

From the presidential palace in Belgrade, Vucic spoke to supporters: "I am resigning as president."

"Tomorrow morning I will hand over my duties to the parliament speaker," he added "This is the last evening for me in this building," Vucic declared.

"I served you faithfully. I served all of you, and our homeland Serbia, honourably and honestly throughout my presidential term," Vucic told supporters. "The fight is only beginning," he added.

Dominating Serbian politics

Vucic is banned by the Serbian Constitution from seeking a third term. He was serving his second term and would have left office in May of 2027.

The 56-year-old, who has ties to Serbian nationalism and had once served as minister under the administration of Slobodan Milosevic, has dominated Serbian politics for more over a decade.

Vucic supporters praise him for his stability, stated commitment to development projects in Serbia and his patriotism, in a country long overshadowed by war in the 1990s and subsequent international isolation.

Opponents, however, have decried what they see as increasingly authoritarian tendencies and leading a government accused of endemic corruption.

Abroad, Vucic has had to juggle the competing interests of his country's European Union aspirations and its close ties to Russia.

Opposition had sought snap elections

Earlier in September, Vucic called for snap elections for October. He cited "major turbulence on the domestic political scene," as the reason.

Vucic was referring to the political movement and major setback for his government that was triggered by a tragedy in Serbia's second-largest city of Novi Sad. In November 2024, an awning of a newly reconstructed railway station in Novi Sad collapsed, killing 16 people.

The disaster triggered nationwide ⁠protests by students and the opposition. They ​demanded accountability for those responsible for the disaster, transparency in public procurement, an end to systemic corruption, and an early parliamentary vote.

Vucic's government repeatedly denied accusations, but still, several officials, including two ministers, were arrested or resigned after the incident. The upcoming snap election will test Vucic's popularity and political survival.

Edited by: Srinivas Mazumdaru, Wesley Dockery

entries.title: Yemen: Houthis report deadly Saudi strikes on Taiz market
entries.summary: The Houthi-run health ministry accused the Saudi Air Force of committing an "abominable crime," vowing to retaliate. The Houthis' account of the attack cannot be independently verified.
entries.content:
Yemen

Yemen: Houthis report deadly Saudi strikes on Taiz market

September 27, 2026

The Houthi-run health ministry accused the Saudi Air Force of committing an "abominable crime," vowing to retaliate. The Houthis' account of the attack cannot be independently verified.

Yemen's Houthi rebels on Sunday accused the Saudi Arabian Air Force of having struck a shopping area around the central market of Taiz. The Iran-aligned Houthis said at least seven people had been killed and dozens injured.

What do we know so far?

The group's Al-Masirah TV channel showed footage of large plumes of smoke and a destroyed warehouse stacked with food in cardboard boxes. Al-Masirah TV also reported that children were among those wounded, citing the Houthis' health ministry.

Taiz is currently under the control of Yemeni government forces, but it has long been besieged by Houthi fighters and remains one of the main fronts in the country's civil war. Taiz is located in southwestern Yemen. 

The escalation in fighting comes after a fragile truce between Yemeni government forces and Houthi rebels broke down months ago and new regional tensions sparked by the Iran war.

The Houthi health ministry accused the Saudi Air Force of committing an "abominable crime," saying it was directly and deliberately targeting civilian sites in Taiz.

Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree accused Saudi Arabia of launching two air raids that hit the market, adding that blood was "unjustly and aggressively spilled" in a statement posted online.

The group has vowed to retaliate.

The claims made by the Houthis cannot be independently verified.

In response to the Houthi report, troops loyal to the internationally recognized government in Yemen confirmed that their air force had struck a Houthi depot and vehicles in the area.

Saudi-backed coalition ramps up attacks after new Houthi offensive

The civil war in Yemen began in 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa from the Saudi-backed government. They went on to take control of vast swaths of the country's north.

Saudi Arabia joined forces against the Houthis the following year, leading an international coalition against them. But so far, Yemen's government forces have not been able to effectively repel the latest Houthi offensive.

Fighting has spiked in September as the Houthis launched a lightning offensive that saw them seize Yemen's entire Red Sea coast. The rebels have also launched a blockade on Saudi energy exports to coincide with Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

Renewed clashes are is under way in several parts of the country, with at least 125,000 people displaced by it.

The Yemeni government has meanwhile called for a general mobilization, urging Yemenis to join the army and security forces. 

Yemen is one of the poorest in the world and remains gripped by a vast humanitarian crisis.

Edited by: Wesley Dockery

entries.title: Avalanche in Nepal leaves 2 dead, several missing
entries.summary: An avalanche has struck the Himlung Himal base camp in Nepal after days of severe weather. Two guides are confirmed dead and at least 14 people remain missing in the remote region.
entries.content:
Nepal

Nepal avalanche kills at least 2, leaves several missing

September 27, 2026

An avalanche has struck the Himlung Himal base camp in Nepal after days of severe weather. Two guides are confirmed dead and at least 14 people remain missing in the remote region.

Two people have died when an avalanche struck the base camp of a mountain in Nepal with at least 14 others still missing. 

The avalanche hit the 7,126-meter (23,380-foot) Himlung Himal after several days of heavy rain and snowfall across the region.

The dead and missing are all mountain guides and staff of Nepalese expedition companies who had been preparing the base camp for paying customers to climb the mountain.

"There were a total of 14 kitchen staff members and two climbing guides from different companies who were missing," the Nepal National Mountain Guide Association said. "The two climbing guides have been found, but sadly, both were found deceased."

Unclear how many are missing

There was conflicting information as to how many people were in the affected area near the border with Tibet at the time of disaster. Local police said there were at least 22 people at the base camp when the avalanche struck on Sunday morning.

Bibhuti Chand Thakur, head of trekking company Himalayan Holidays Nepal, told news agency DPA that search and rescue operations were under way. "The chance of survival remains high because of fresh snow," he said, adding that he did not yet have a definitive number of missing or survivors, as the area is remote and cut off from communication.

Authorities had warned of severe weather across Nepal over the weekend. Rain has affected much of the country since Thursday, with snowfall reported in the higher northern regions. The conditions have disrupted roads and trekking routes and led authorities to suspend climbing and trekking activities on several mountains.

The Himalayan nation is home to eight of the world's 14 mountains higher than 8,000 meters, and trekking and mountaineering tourism is vital to the country's economy.

The latest avalanche comes as Nepal continues to recover from devastating floods in August that killed more than 1,400 people and left thousands missing.

Edited by: Wesley Dockery

entries.title: UK: 5 arrested after 'major incident' near Fairford air base
entries.summary: Scores of homes were evacuated in the UK town of Whelford, near an air base used by the US military, with bomb disposal teams checking "suspicious vehicles" at the scene. Police said five men had been arrested.
entries.content:
September 27, 2026

Scores of homes were evacuated in the UK town of Whelford, near an air base used by the US military, with bomb disposal teams checking "suspicious vehicles" at the scene. Police said five men had been arrested.

British authorities evacuated buildings and deployed military bomb disposal teams over a "major incident" in the town of Whelford on Sunday morning.

London's Metropolitan police said five men were arrested on suspicion of preparing a "terrorist act" and explosive-related offenses.

The town is located near the Fairford air base, which is used by the US military. Around 30 emergency vehicles were seen in the area, including police cars, ambulances, and fire engines. The authorities said they believed the incident to be "contained."

Counter-terrorism police were leading the probe.

"We are in the early stages of an investigation," Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans said in an online statement, adding that the authorities were "working closely with our partners" to understand the circumstances of the incident.

The statement urged the public to share any information they may have related to the issue.

Praise from Trump and Burnham

US President Donald Trump praised those involved in the arrests. “It was an amazing job," he told reporters in the US.

"We had them under investigation. They were looking to do big damage to our fort. And working with the British worked out great," Trump said.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he understood that the incident would be "deeply concerning" for many people.

In a social media post, Burnham thanked the police and armed forces for their response and expressed his gratitude to residents who had been evacuated from their homes "while precautionary checks are carried out."

Bomb disposal units examining three 'suspicious vehicles'

Local police said they had received a call overnight on Sunday about "three suspicious vehicles" heading to the base.

"Armed officers responded and subsequently arrested five men in the Whelford area," assistant chief constable Richard Ocone told reporters.

He added that a cordon of 400 meters, or approximately 1/4 of a mile, has been put in place around the vehicles "while the army's explosive ordinance disposal unit examine them."

"As a precaution, around 85 households have been advised to evacuate while these examinations take place," Ocone said.

He added that some of the evacuees were taken to a nearby leisure center.

The Gloucestershire police representative also asked the public "not to speculate" but follow official channels instead.

Officials stay tight-lipped

A spokesperson for ​the US Air Force refused to discuss specific steps when contacted by the Reuters news agency, saying only that both US and British forces "remain vigilant and will take ⁠appropriate ​actions to ensure the safety and security of our ​US service members, civilians, contractors, and their families."

The background for the incident was not immediately clear.

The UK has allowed the US to use Fairford for its war against Iran, with Iran's Revolutionary Guards warning UK officials against the move this summer. The evacuations also come at a time of heightened tensions in Northern Ireland, and less than two months after Germany discovered an explosive-laden drone at the Leipzig airport, which its authorities attributed to Russia.

Edited by: Sean Sinico and Wesley Dockery

entries.title: Two people killed as bus crashes on way to Oktoberfest
entries.summary: The bus was traveling from Italy to Munich, carrying 33 Filipino tourists who wanted to visit the famous beer festival. One of the dozens injured remains in life-threatening condition.
entries.content:
Germany

Two people killed after bus crashes on way to Oktoberfest

September 27, 2026

The bus was traveling from Italy to Munich, carrying 33 Filipino tourists who wanted to visit the famous beer festival. One of the dozens injured remains in life-threatening condition.

Two people were killed and many more injured when a bus carrying a group of Filipino tourists overturned in southern Germany on Sunday en route to the Munich Oktoberfest.

The bus was coming from Milan, an Italian city with a large Filipino community.

According to German police, there were 33 tourists on the bus when, at 5:41 a.m. local time (03:41 a.m. GMT), the vehicle went off the side of the A96 highway and overturned. No other vehicles were involved in the crash.

Six of the injured were immediately rushed by helicopter to nearby hospitals, one of whom was thought to still be in a life-threatening condition. Two more were taken by ambulance to the hospital, while another 22 were first treated at the scene before several of those were also brought to the hospital.

Police so far have only identified one of the two people who died as a 58-year-old Filipino citizen.

"It is naturally very chaotic at first, and establishing the facts is difficult,” explained a spokesperson for the local police headquarters. It took police hours to confirm how many people actually were on the bus.

Bus driver charged with negligent homicide

In addition to the 33 tourists, there were the two Italian bus drivers on board, both of whom were not injured in the crash. The driver who was at the wheel at the time of the crash is now being investigated for negligent homicide, police said. "That is standard procedure,” a police spokeswoman explained.

The cause of the accident remained unclear, police said. "The public prosecutor's office has commissioned an accident reconstruction expert report to determine the cause of the crash. It is far too early to comment.”

More than 200 firefighters, medics and police were rushed to the scene of the crash. A section of the highway was completely blocked for some time before, but in the afternoon, traffic was allowed to resume.

There have been a string of bus accidents in recent weeks. Earlier in September, a Dutch coach crashed in Switzerland, killing five, while a bus crash on Germany's A3 highway left 30 people injured.

Oktoberfest draws millions of visitors

Munich’s Oktoberfest is the world’s largest beer festival, attracting millions of visitors to the Bavarian capital each year. Held over roughly two weeks, it combines giant beer tents, traditional Bavarian food, live music and fairground rides, drawing visitors from Germany and around the world.

This year, the Oktoberfest runs from September 19 to October 4. Organizers said that at the halfway point, around 3.8 million people had already visited the festival — about 300,000 more than at the same point last year.

Edited by: Wesley Dockery

entries.title: Pope decries 'scourge' of sexual abuse during France visit
entries.summary: French bishops took "courageous" steps when faced with "the painful scourge of abuse of minors," Pope Leo XIV told the high-ranking clerics before his scheduled meeting with survivors at the Catholic shrine of Lourdes.
entries.content:
France

Pope decries 'scourge' of sexual abuse during France visit

September 27, 2026

French bishops took "courageous" steps when faced with "the painful scourge of abuse of minors," Pope Leo XIV told the high-ranking clerics before his scheduled meeting with survivors at the Catholic shrine of Lourdes.

Around 150,000 attended the Mass celebrated by Pope Leo at the shrine of Lourdes during the third day of his four-day visit to France.

The shrine, located near the Spanish border, is venerated by Catholics as a place of healing. Many victims of sexual abuse have also traveled to the site in recent years as they seek to recover from their trauma.

On Sunday, Leo urged respect for life, including for the sick and frail, in what was seen as veiled criticism of euthanasia and abortion.

"Your crutches, your wheelchairs and your hidden tears are not obstacles; instead, they are the very place where you are fully respected and welcomed," Leo said. "Lourdes is blessed as a place for professing the beauty and sanctity of life, for life is welcomed here as a precious gift from God."

Later, the pope also said it was "impossible to regard causing death as something normal."

"What is legal is not necessarily moral," he added, in what could be seen as a reference to France's euthanasia and assisted suicide law which came into effect last month.

"We must reject the temptation to cause death under the guise of false compassion," said the 71-year-old pontiff.

Hundreds of thousands of children abused in France alone

The head of the Catholic Church was due to meet with seven adult survivors of sexual abuse on Sunday — part of Vatican's decadeslong reckoning with the widespread molestation of children at the hands of the clergy and the steps senior Church figures have taken to cover up the scandal in many countries around the world.

A 2021 report found that around 330,000 children had been abused by Catholic priests and lay leaders between 1950 and 2020 in France.

While not directly referencing the issue during his Mass in Lourdes, the religious leader called for humility among the clergy's ranks.

"The admission of our mistakes is indispensable for our spiritual growth," Leo told the crowd. "In order to heal the deep wounds, infidelities and painful errors that have occurred within (the Church), we must humbly place ourselves under the Lord's purifying gaze."

But some survivors expressed doubt that the pope's visit would lead to quick changes within the church.

"Things are moving very slowly," Michele Le Reun-Gaigne, a co-leader of a French survivors' association, told the Reuters news agency. "It isn't going to happen overnight."

Pope urges 'vigilance' while meeting bishops

Earlier on Sunday, the pope met with French bishops and praised their "courageous" response to "the painful scourge of abuse committed against minors by members of the clergy or in an ecclesial context."

He thanked the bishops for "listening, the search for truth, justice, forgiveness and making amends" and praised their "firm commitment to a culture of prevention and protection against these crimes."

 "You must continue along the path you have begun, maintaining the greatest vigilance," the US-born pope said, according to the readout provided by the Vatican.

Edited by: Sean Sinico and Wesley Dockery

entries.title: European cities seek ways of boosting affordable housing
entries.summary: In many major urban centers of Europe, the housing shortage has become an explosive social issue. DW looks into various models that have been put in place across the continent.
entries.content:
France

European cities seek ways of boosting affordable housing

September 27, 2026

In many major urban centers of Europe, the housing shortage has become an explosive social issue. DW looks into various models that have been put in place across the continent.

In the European Union's most populous city, pressure on the housing market is so great that many of its residents are willing to undertake a historic experiment: Five years ago, Berliners voted in a referendum to instruct the Senate of the German capital to draft a law that would put an end to the power of large real estate companies. Those that owned more than 3,000 units should be expropriated, they said. The Senate did not act on the results of the referendum, which was non-binding. Meanwhile, the average cost of new leases has since risen by about half.

But in the Berlin elections on September 20, the socialist Left Party, which in its campaign had promised to act on the referendum, won the largest share of the vote. Whether it will be able to make good on its promises now depends on how negotiations to form a coalition shape up. But whatever happens, the election has drawn attention once again to the severity of the housing crisis in many cities across Europe.

Here are some initiatives that have already been put in place:

Vienna: The city is the landlord

The Vienna model is a flagship solution to soaring rent prices in Europe. The ambitious social housing program as introduced after World War I when the Austrian capital experienced a severe housing crisis. Beds were so scarce that some workers had to sleep in shifts. Diseases such as tuberculosis spread in the cramped living conditions. 

The model serves to stabilize the city's housing market to this day: According to the Vienna authorities, the city owns approximately 220,000 municipal apartments that it rents out as well as 200,000 subsidized dwellings. More than 60% of Vienna's residents live in one of these two types of housing. This also helps to stabilize prices on the private market.

Basel: Public land, private buildings

The fact that housing is becoming increasingly expensive in many cities is largely due to the fact that a city's attractiveness is reflected in land prices. In many places, people are considering how to decouple rents from the price of land. One means of doing this is not to sell municipal land but to lease it to cooperatives or socially-conscious investors. This benefits councils that do not have to bear construction costs and developers too, as they do not have to factor in exorbitant land costs that are ultimately passed on to tenants.

The Swiss city of Basel is one of the pioneers of this model. About 40% of all cooperative housing units are located on public land. The Spanish city of Barcelona and the Portuguese capital Lisbon have also stepped up efforts to put this model in place.

Paris: Buying back office buildings and converting them into homes

It is harder if land and buildings are in private hands. In 2014, the French capital Paris launched an anti-displacement plan giving the municipality a "first right of refusal" in gentrifying neighborhoods to increase the share of affordable housing in the city. The current target is 30% social housing for low-income residents by 2035

Earlier this year, the French government and the Paris regional authorities identified 61 projects that could convert empty office buildings into housing and create up to 8,200 homes in the inner suburbs of the French capital.

Prague: Apartments for public-sector workers

The Czech capital has found another way to keep those without whom the city could not function in Prague: caregivers, police officers, teachers and sanitation workers. Some 660 new energy-efficient apartments reserved specifically for public-sector employees have just been built.

The subsidiary of a Czech bank, which has received European loans, handled the development. The aim is to keep rents 20% below the market rate thanks to economies of scale, and it is not the bank who decides on the tenants but hospitals or public sector agencies, which draw up leases and can attract new employees with affordable rent options. More apartments are currently being planned.

Dublin: Non-profit cost rental housing

It has also become difficult for people with low incomes to stay in the Irish capital Dublin. During and after Ireland's financial crisis of 2008, foreign investors bought up a lot of real estate and at the same time rents skyrocketed when several major tech companies chose Dublin as their EU headquarters because of favorable tax rates. There are now long waiting lists for public housing in the city whose supply remains too low.

In 2021, the Irish government introduced the Cost Rental Housing program to provide housing to those on middle incomes, i.e. those who earn too much to qualify for public housing but too little to have a chance on the private market. To qualify in Dublin, a household has to have a net income of below €66,000 ($75,000) per year. Non-profits or public agencies lease out the apartments and rents are below market levels, by an average of almost 30% according to a recent study by the Dublin-based Economic & Social Research Institute (ESRI).

The Irish government hopes to be able to deliver 18,000 low-cost rental homes by the end of the decade. Last year, there were more than 4,200 applicants for 104 apartments in a new community in a suburb of Dublin.

This article was translated from German.

entries.title: Switzerland: Voters reject stricter view of neutrality
entries.summary: Early projections show Swiss voters rejecting a stricter application of the country's vaunted neutrality. Swiss neutrality has been enshrined in the constitution since 1848.
entries.content:
Switzerland

Switzerland: Voters reject stricter view of neutrality

September 27, 2026

Early projections show Swiss voters rejecting a stricter application of the country's vaunted neutrality. Swiss neutrality has been enshrined in the constitution since 1848.

Voters in Switzerland   look set to reject a proposal for stricter neutrality in a referendum held on Sunday, according to projections by state broadcaster SRF.

According to SRF figures, 29% voted for tighter rules on neutrality while 71% voted against adopting stricter measures.

Although Swiss ‌neutrality has ⁠been recognized since the end of the Napoleonic wars in 1815 and part of the country's constitution since 1848, exactly how the government implements it is not clearly specified.

The initiative was brought forward by the Pro Schweiz association, a right-wing organization with links to the right-wing populist Swiss People's Party. They argue that the Swiss government has moved too close to the European Union and NATO since Russia's war in Ukraine.

What the Pro Schweiz Association wanted to achieve

The group said its aims were for:

  • Swiss neutrality to be applied "permanently and without exception"
  • Switzerland to maintain an army capable of defense
  • Switzerland not to get involved in conflicts between third parties
  • Switzerland not to join a defense alliance unless attacked
  • The UN to approve any sanctions before Switzerland joins them

Swiss sentiment on neutrality

According to a poll by the Swiss Broadcasting Corporation (SBC) earlier this month, the move toward a stricter interpretation of Swiss neutrality does not have the traction needed to pass a referendum. Some 63% of respondents said they intend to vote against the initiative, while 34% plan on backing it.

Nearly all major political parties rejected the initiative, with the exception of the hard-right Swiss People's Party (SVP).

"Our goal is to foster peace, diplomacy and dialogue," SVP vice president Celine Amaudruz said during a televised debate. "To achieve that, we must maintain credibility through perpetual armed neutrality."

Swiss foreign minister: Neutrality needs 'degree of flexibility'

Opponents of the initiative argued that in the modern world a country cannot hide behind neutrality and treat perpetrators and victims equally.

"Neutrality has always been applied with a degree of flexibility," Swiss Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis insisted during a recent televised debate.

In-person voting will begin at 10:00 am (0800 GMT) and polling stations close at noon. The result should become clear around an hour later.

Another referendum on food security has also taken place with that initiative calling for the Swiss population to have access to enough high-quality and affordable food at all times.

According to SRF figures 28% of voters supported the initiative and 72% rejected it.

The food initiative seeks to have Switzerland produce significantly more of its own food.
